link.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 1: image classification and nearest neighbours

entry.content:
Series · Deep learning for computer vision 1Image classification and nearest neighbours 2Linear classifiers and loss functions 3Optimisation 4Backpropagation and neural networks 5Convolutional networks 6Visualising and understanding 7CNN architectures · soon 8Detection and segmentation · soon 9Vision transformers · soon

You glance at a photo and know at once that it shows a cat. To a computer the same photo is a grid of numbers, one per pixel per colour. Nothing in that grid says “cat”. The same cat in a different pose, under a different light or half behind a sofa gives a completely different grid. People call this the semantic gap, and closing it is what computer vision is about.

This series is a tour of how deep learning closes it. It follows the order of Stanford’s course CS231n: Deep Learning for Computer Vision, and its course notes. Each part takes one stretch of the course and builds it from scratch. Every figure runs the real model in your browser, and every number you see is computed, not drawn by hand.

This first part follows the course’s opening topic, image classification: what the problem is, and the simplest method that solves it at all, nearest neighbours.

The photos

CS231n works with CIFAR-10: 60,000 colour photos of 32 × 32 pixels, in ten classes (planes, cars, birds, cats, …). This series uses a small slice of it, small enough to download with the page and run in your browser:

  • four of the classes: plane, car, frog and ship;
  • 320 training photos (80 per class), 80 more for validation, and 100 for testing.

Each photo is 32 × 32 pixels, and each pixel has three numbers, for red, green and blue: 3,072 numbers per photo. They’re tiny, but you can still tell a frog from a ship, which is the point: whatever a computer does with them, you can check it with your own eyes.

Classifying by nearest neighbours, step by step

This is what the computer gets. You see a jet against a blue sky. The computer sees, for each of the 1,024 pixels, three numbers from 0 to 255: how much red, green and blue light it has. The framed patch, on the jet’s wing, is light grey: all three numbers are high, the blue a little lower.

The task of image classification is to take those 3,072 numbers and return one label from a fixed list: here plane, car, frog or ship.

Try writing the rule yourself. “A plane has wings and a tail” is easy to say. Turning it into arithmetic on pixel values, for every size, angle, colour and background of plane, is hopeless.

The data-driven approach. Instead of writing rules, collect many photos that people have already labelled, and let an algorithm learn from them.

Every classifier in this series has the same two parts:

  1. train(images, labels) → a model,
  2. predict(model, image) → a label.

Here are 12 training photos of each class. The coloured tab on top of each is its label. Notice how much they vary: planes in the sky and on the ground, cars of every colour, frogs on rock, leaves and white paper.

The simplest model: remember everything. Training just stores all 320 photos. To predict, find the stored photo most like the new one and copy its label.

To say what “most like” means, we need a distance. The simplest is the L1 distance: subtract the two photos number by number, drop the signs, and add up all 3,072 differences (with each number scaled to run from 0 to 1).

\[d_1(I_1, I_2) = \sum_{p} \lvert I_1^p - I_2^p \rvert\]

The third picture shows the differences: dark where the two photos disagree, white where they match. Scroll to watch the sum build up, row by row. Identical photos are 0 apart; these two are 304.7 apart.

Now measure the distance to all 320 training photos and sort them, nearest first. Here are the 24 nearest; each caption is the distance.

The nearest photo, ringed, is a ship, so the nearest neighbour classifier says “ship”. It’s wrong.

Look at what the near photos have in common: not wings, but a pale blue background. Sky and sea are both pale blue, and the background fills most of the pixels, so to L1 distance a plane in the sky and a boat on the water look alike. The jet itself barely counts.

Use ◀ ▶ above the figure to try other test photos.

Ask more than one neighbour. The k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) classifier takes the k nearest training photos and lets them vote.

With k = 3 the vote is 2 ship, 1 plane: still wrong. Move the slider to k = 5 and the next two neighbours, both planes, tip it to plane, 3 to 2.

You can also switch to the L2 distance, the straight-line distance \(\sqrt{\sum_p (I_1^p - I_2^p)^2}\). It squares the differences, so it punishes one big difference more than many small ones. Here it reorders the neighbours enough that k = 3 already says plane.

k and the distance are hyperparameters: choices we make, not things the algorithm learns. How do we pick them?

Not by trying them on the test photos. If we pick whichever setting scores best on the test set, the test score stops being an honest estimate of how we’ll do on new photos. The test set gets used once, at the very end.

Instead, we set aside a validation set: 80 more labelled photos, kept out of training. The chart tries every k from 1 to 15 on them (solid L1, dashed L2).

L1 with k = 8 does best: 48 of 80 (60%) right. Run once on the 100 test photos, it gets 53%. A random guess would get 25%, so k-NN has learned something. But not much: it gets 20 of the 25 frogs and only 2 of the 25 cars, and it calls 12 of the cars frogs.

Why so bad? Take this plane, and make three copies: one moved 2 pixels right, one a little darker, and one with a black square covering its middle. Each copy is about 570 away from the original in L1 distance.

To you the first two are obviously the same plane, and the third a damaged one. To the distance they’re all equally different, and all three are further from the original than a photo of a frog, at 556: the nearest photo in the whole training set.

The trouble isn’t k or the choice of L1 or L2. Distances between raw pixels measure the wrong thing: they compare colours at fixed positions, not what the photo shows. The CS231n notes make the same point with the same three kinds of edit, using L2.

The whole thing in one line

For a test image \(x\), k-NN finds the \(k\) training images \(x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_k}\) nearest to it, and predicts the label that appears most often among \(y_{i_1}, \dots, y_{i_k}\).

It has two odd properties.

Training is free, and predicting is slow. Training only stores the data. Predicting compares the test image with every training image. With \(N\) training images of \(D\) pixels:

  work in our slice on all of CIFAR-10
train store \(N\) images 320 photos 50,000 photos
predict \(N \cdot D\) differences 320 × 3,072 ≈ 1 million 50,000 × 3,072 ≈ 154 million

That’s backwards from what we want. We can afford to train for a long time, once; we need predictions to be fast, on a phone, thousands of times a second.

It doesn’t work well on real images. We got 53% on four classes. On all ten classes of CIFAR-10, with all 50,000 training photos, the course notes report 38.6% with L1 and 35.4% with L2. People get about 94%, and convolutional networks about 95%.

What’s still missing

  • Predicting needs the whole training set. A model should be a small summary of the data, not the data itself.
  • Distances between raw pixels don’t measure what an image shows. Move, darken or partly cover an image and its pixel distance changes a lot, while its meaning doesn’t change at all.

Part 2 fixes the first problem with a linear classifier: a model that boils the training set down to one template per class, so predicting is one quick calculation. The second problem takes us until part 5, where convolutional networks learn features that look at shapes, not at where the colours sit.

Going deeper

What k does to the boundaries

On photos it’s hard to see the decision regions, because they live in 3,072 dimensions. On points in the plane we can paint them. Below, each spot is coloured by the class k-NN would give a new point placed there. Three points sit deliberately in the “wrong” blob.

With k = 1 every training point owns its own patch, so each odd point carves an island out of its neighbours’ region. The boundary follows the noise. As k grows, the islands vanish and the boundaries smooth out.

That is the classic trade-off. Small k: the model fits the training data exactly, noise included (overfitting). Large k: it smooths away real detail (underfitting). The caption scores each setting by leave-one-out accuracy: each point is classified by all the others, an extreme form of the cross-validation below.

L1 or L2?

Both are reasonable; they differ in which images they call close.

  • L2 squares each difference, so one large difference counts for more than several small ones adding up to the same total. It prefers images that differ a little everywhere.
  • L1 treats all differences alike. It’s also tied to the axes: rotate the coordinate system and L1 distances change, while L2 distances don’t. For pixels, which have fixed meaning, that hardly matters.

In the 2-D figure above, L1’s regions have borders at 45° and straight angles; L2’s are straight lines at any angle. On our photos, L1 picks k = 8 and scores 53% on the test set; L2 picks k = 12 and scores 51%. On CIFAR-10, too, L1 does slightly better.

Cross-validation

With only 320 training photos, a validation set of 80 is expensive: it’s data we didn’t train on. k-fold cross-validation reuses it:

  1. Split the training data into, say, 5 equal folds.
  2. For each fold: train on the other 4, measure accuracy on this one.
  3. Average the 5 accuracies, and pick the hyperparameters with the best average.

Every image gets used for both training and validation, just never at the same time. It costs 5 times as much computation, so it’s mostly used when data is scarce. With large datasets and slow models, people use a single validation split, as we did.

The curse of dimensionality

k-NN works when every test point has close training neighbours. That needs the training points to fill the space densely, and the amount of data needed grows exponentially with the number of dimensions.

Divide each axis into 4 bins. In 1 dimension you need 4 points to put one in every bin; in 2 dimensions, 16; in 64 dimensions, \(4^{64} \approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}\). Our 32 × 32 × 3 photos have 3,072 dimensions.

So nearest-neighbour methods only work in high dimensions if the data isn’t really spread across all of them. Images aren’t: natural images fill a tiny part of the space of all pixel grids. But “nearby in that part” is still badly measured by raw pixel distance, as the moved, darkened and covered planes showed.

Nearest neighbours are not dead

k-NN on raw pixels is a poor classifier, but k-NN itself is everywhere in modern vision. The trick is to measure distance between features a network computed, not pixels. Image search, face recognition and “find similar products” all embed images with a deep network, then look up nearest neighbours among millions of stored embeddings.

To make that fast, they use approximate nearest-neighbour search, which finds almost the nearest points while skipping most of the comparisons, as in the FAISS library. Part 5’s convolutional networks are where such features come from.

Further reading

  • CS231n notes, Image Classification: the data-driven approach, k-NN and validation on CIFAR-10.
  • T. Cover and P. Hart, Nearest neighbor pattern classification (1967): the classic analysis of the 1-NN rule.
  • A. Krizhevsky, Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images (2009): the report that introduced CIFAR-10.
  • J. Johnson, M. Douze and H. Jégou, Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs (2017): nearest neighbours at scale, the FAISS library.

entry.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 2: linear classifiers and loss functions

link.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 2: linear classifiers and loss functions

entry.content:
Series · Deep learning for computer vision 1Image classification and nearest neighbours 2Linear classifiers and loss functions 3Optimisation 4Backpropagation and neural networks 5Convolutional networks 6Visualising and understanding 7CNN architectures · soon 8Detection and segmentation · soon 9Vision transformers · soon

In part 1, k-nearest neighbours classified our photos of planes, cars, frogs and ships by comparing each new one with all 320 training photos. It got 53% right, against 25% for guessing, but it had to keep the whole training set around, and every prediction compared against all of it.

This part follows the next stretch of CS231n, linear classification. Instead of storing the training photos, we’ll learn a fixed set of numbers from them: one template per class. A prediction is then one quick calculation, however much data we trained on.

Two ideas come with it, and the rest of the series uses both:

  • a score function, which turns an image into one score per class,
  • a loss function, which says, with a single number, how unhappy we are with those scores.

Part 3 will add the third piece, optimisation: how to find the template values that make the loss small. In this part the classifier is already trained, so we can look at what it learned. (It was trained before you opened the page, on the same 320 photos, by 1,500 steps of the gradient descent part 3 explains. Every number in the figure is then computed from its weights in your browser.)

A linear classifier, step by step

A linear classifier sees an image as one long list of numbers. Read the photo’s 32 rows one after another, three numbers (red, green, blue) per pixel, and the 32 × 32 grid becomes a list \(x\) of 3,072 numbers. The strip in the figure is that list, drawn as colours.

That throws away the fact that some pixels are neighbours. The classifier will only know that number 1,000 and number 1,003 are different inputs. We’ll come back to this; part 5 builds it back in.

The test photo here is a plane on a runway that this classifier gets wrong. That makes it a good one to learn from. Use ◀ ▶ above to switch photos.

For each class, the classifier has 3,072 weights and one bias. Its score for that class is

\[s_j = w_j \cdot x + b_j = \sum_{p=1}^{3072} w_{j,p}\, x_p + b_j\]

Each number in the photo is multiplied by its weight, and the 3,072 products are added up. The middle panel adds up each pixel’s three products and shows the result, one class at a time: red pixels push the score up, blue pixels push it down.

Stack the four weight rows into a 4 × 3,072 matrix \(W\), and all four scores come from one matrix–vector product: \(s = Wx + b\). The predicted class is the one with the highest score.

One detail, which CS231n does too: before anything else, the average training photo is subtracted from every photo. So a number in \(x\) says how much brighter or darker that spot is than usual, and can be negative.

Here the plane scores 0.25 and the car 0.38, but the ship wins with 1.60. That’s wrong.

Fold each class’s 3,072 weights back into a 32 × 32 colour picture, and you can see what the classifier learned. Each one is a template: the score is high when the photo looks like it. The pictures stretch each template’s weights to fill the range from dark to light, as the CS231n notes do.

They are noisy. With only 80 training photos per class, the classifier latches onto whatever happened to tell those particular photos apart. But some of it reads. The frog template is green and brown all over, the colours of a frog in the grass. The ship template is blue, especially at the edges and the bottom: sea. The car template has a red-purple blob low in the middle, where a car’s body sits.

The deeper problem is that one template has to stand for every plane: nose left or right, on a runway or in the sky, white or green. It can only be a blur of them. Our plane on the runway is a long, light, horizontal shape between sky and tarmac; in the previous step, the ship’s weights scored that band in red.

Still, the classifier gets 67% of the test photos right (14 planes, 14 cars, 21 frogs and 18 ships out of 25 each), against 53% for k-NN. And it needs only 12,292 numbers instead of all 320 photos.

Another way to see it: each photo is a point in a 3,072-dimensional space, and the classifier cuts that space into regions with flat walls.

We can’t draw 3,072 dimensions, so here is the same classifier on points with just 2 numbers each. The tint shows which class wins at every spot.

Where two classes’ scores are equal, \(w_i \cdot x + b_i = w_j \cdot x + b_j\), which is a straight line. So every border between regions is straight. On these three blobs that’s all we need: every point is on the right side.

How bad were the scores for our plane? A loss function turns that question into one number.

The multiclass SVM loss wants the true class’s score to beat every wrong class’s score by at least a margin of 1. For each wrong class \(j\) it charges however far short of that we fell:

\[L = \sum_{j \neq y} \max(0,\; s_j - s_y + 1)\]

For our plane (\(s_y\) = 0.25):

  • car: 0.38 − 0.25 + 1 = 1.13, so it costs 1.13.
  • frog: −2.23 − 0.25 + 1 is below 0, so it costs nothing. The plane already beats it by more than the margin.
  • ship: 1.60 − 0.25 + 1 = 2.35.

The loss is 3.48. If the plane’s score beat every other score by 1 or more, it would be 0.

The other common loss reads the scores as probabilities. Scores can be any number, so first make them positive by exponentiating, then divide by their sum so they add up to 1. That’s the softmax function:

\[p_j = \frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_k e^{s_k}}\]

Our plane gets probability 0.165, and ship gets 0.634. The cross-entropy loss is the negative log of the true class’s probability:

\[L = -\log p_y = -\log 0.165 = 1.80\]

If the true class got probability 1, the loss would be 0; as its probability falls towards 0, the loss grows without limit. This softmax classifier is the one CS231n uses most, and every network in the rest of this series ends with it.

The loss on the training data isn’t all we care about. Many different \(W\) can fit the training photos about equally well, and we’d like the one most likely to work on new photos.

Regularisation adds a penalty for large weights to the loss:

\[L = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} L_i + \frac{\lambda}{2} \sum_{j,p} W_{j,p}^2\]

The bigger \(\lambda\), the more the classifier is pushed towards small, spread-out weights. Pick a value under the figure and watch the templates change.

With no penalty (\(\lambda\) = 0), the classifier gets 99% of its training photos right but only 62.5% of the validation photos: it has memorised noise, and its templates look like it. That gap is overfitting. At \(\lambda\) = 0.1, training accuracy falls to 87% and validation rises to 70%, the best of the four; that’s the classifier the other steps use. Push further and the templates turn into smooth, readable blurs (a pale sky with a dark shape in the middle for the plane, deep blue for the ship), but the classifier is now too constrained to fit even its training photos: 68% at \(\lambda\) = 1, 59% at \(\lambda\) = 10.

As with k in part 1, \(\lambda\) is chosen on the validation photos, never the test ones.

Here is the limit in a picture. These three classes are arms of a spiral. Every arm winds around the others, so no set of straight borders can separate them.

The best linear classifier gets 52% of the points right, against 33% for guessing. The CS231n notes get 49% on their version of this spiral.

No choice of loss or regularisation can fix this. The scores themselves have to become something more flexible than \(Wx + b\). That’s what neural networks do, in part 4.

The whole thing in one line

A linear classifier computes one score per class,

\[s = W x + b\]

with \(x\) the image as a list of \(D\) numbers, \(W\) a \(C \times D\) matrix of weights and \(b\) a list of \(C\) biases. Learning means finding the \(W\) and \(b\) that make the total loss small:

\[L(W, b) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} L_i\big(s(x_i), y_i\big) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \lVert W \rVert^2\]

where \(L_i\) is the SVM loss or the cross-entropy loss of one training example.

Compared with k-NN:

  k-NN linear classifier
what it keeps all \(N\) training images \(C \times D + C\) numbers
our photos 320 × 3,072 ≈ 983,000 numbers 4 × 3,072 + 4 = 12,292
on CIFAR-10 50,000 × 3,072 ≈ 154 million 10 × 3,072 + 10 = 30,730
cost to predict \(N \cdot D\) \(C \cdot D\)
test accuracy (ours) 53% 67%

What’s still missing

  • We haven’t said how to find \(W\). The models in the figure were trained, but by what? That’s part 3: gradient descent.
  • One template per class is too few. It can’t say “a plane, facing either way, anywhere in the picture”.
  • Straight borders are too few. The spiral needs curved ones.

Going deeper

The bias trick

Carrying \(W\) and \(b\) around separately is clumsy. Append a constant 1 to every input, \(x' = (x_1, \dots, x_D, 1)\), and add \(b\) as an extra column of \(W\):

\[W x + b = \begin{bmatrix} W & b \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Now the classifier is a single matrix product. In practice, libraries keep \(b\) separate, but the derivations get shorter with the trick.

Scale makes the margin arbitrary

The SVM margin of 1 looks like a choice we’d have to tune. It isn’t. Multiply \(W\) and \(b\) by 2 and every score doubles, so every score difference doubles too: a classifier that beats the margin of 1 by a bit now beats it by more. The size of the weights and the size of the margin trade off against each other, and the regularisation strength \(\lambda\) is what really sets how far apart the scores end up. So the margin can be fixed at 1 and only \(\lambda\) tuned.

Scaling the scores changes the softmax

The softmax doesn’t just look at which score is highest; it looks at how far apart they are. Scale our plane’s scores by a factor \(c\) and watch the probabilities:

As \(c \to 0\) the probabilities all approach \(\frac{1}{4}\); as \(c\) grows, the top score takes everything. So the softmax loss can always be lowered by scaling up a \(W\) that already gets an example right, which is one more reason regularisation is needed to keep the weights finite.

SVM or softmax?

They usually give classifiers that perform about the same. The difference is in what satisfies them.

  • The SVM loss is happy as soon as every margin is met: the frog term above is exactly 0, and nothing more is learned from it.
  • The softmax loss is never fully happy: a probability of 0.98 can still be pushed to 0.99. Every example keeps contributing a little.

The softmax also gives numbers that read as confidence, which is useful downstream, though deep networks’ probabilities tend to be overconfident.

A sanity check at the start

When training starts, the weights are tiny random numbers, so every score is close to 0. That tells you what the first loss should be:

  • SVM: every wrong class gives \(\max(0, 0 - 0 + 1) = 1\), so \(L \approx C - 1\). With our 4 classes, that’s 3; our untrained classifier’s average loss is 3.03.
  • Softmax: every class gets probability \(\frac{1}{C}\), so \(L \approx \log C\). With 4 classes, \(\log 4 = 1.386\); ours is 1.400.

If your first loss is far from these, something in the code is wrong. CS231n suggests this check before every training run.

Why squared weights?

Take an input \(x = (1, 1, 1, 1)\) and two weight vectors, \(w_1 = (1, 0, 0, 0)\) and \(w_2 = (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)\). Both give the same score, \(w \cdot x = 1\). The L2 penalty is 1 for \(w_1\) and 0.25 for \(w_2\), so regularisation prefers \(w_2\): use all the evidence a little, instead of one pixel a lot. A single noisy pixel then can’t swing the decision. That’s what the templates show as \(\lambda\) grows: speckle gives way to broad patches of colour.

The L1 penalty, \(\sum \lvert W_{j,p} \rvert\), does the opposite: it pushes many weights to exactly zero, which selects a few inputs. Both are used; L2 is the default for neural networks, where it’s also called weight decay.

Where the cross-entropy comes from

Two readings of the same formula:

  • Probability. Treat the softmax outputs as the model’s probabilities. The probability the model gives to the whole training set is \(\prod_i p_{y_i}\). Making that large is the same as making \(-\sum_i \log p_{y_i}\) small. So minimising cross-entropy is maximum likelihood.
  • Information. The cross-entropy between the true distribution \(q\) (all of its mass on the right class) and the model’s \(p\) is \(H(q, p) = -\sum_j q_j \log p_j = -\log p_y\). It’s smallest when \(p = q\).

Adding the L2 penalty also has a probability reading: it’s a Gaussian prior on the weights, which makes training a maximum a posteriori estimate.

Further reading

  • CS231n notes, Linear classification: Support Vector Machine, Softmax: the same material on all ten CIFAR-10 classes, with an interactive demo.
  • A. Krizhevsky, Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images (2009): the CIFAR-10 dataset our photos come from.
  • J. Weston and C. Watkins, Support Vector Machines for Multi-Class Pattern Recognition (ESANN 1999): the multiclass SVM loss used here.
  • C. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006), chapter 4: linear models for classification, including the softmax and its probabilistic reading.

entry.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 3: optimisation

link.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 3: optimisation

entry.content:
Series · Deep learning for computer vision 1Image classification and nearest neighbours 2Linear classifiers and loss functions 3Optimisation 4Backpropagation and neural networks 5Convolutional networks 6Visualising and understanding 7CNN architectures · soon 8Detection and segmentation · soon 9Vision transformers · soon

Part 2 built a classifier from two pieces: a score function with weights \(W\), and a loss that says how bad its scores are. It skipped the question of how the weights get their values.

That’s optimisation: find the weights that make the loss as small as possible. This part follows CS231n’s lecture on regularisation and optimisation. The same few methods train everything from part 2’s linear classifier to networks with billions of weights.

A landscape you can see

The loss is a function of the weights. Part 2’s classifier had 12,292 weights, so its loss is a surface over a 12,292-dimensional space, which no one can draw.

So this part shrinks the classifier until the surface fits on screen: two weights, \(w_1\) and \(w_2\), and no bias. It looks at 80 points, each with two numbers \(x = (x_1, x_2)\), in two classes, and gives each point the probability \(p = \sigma(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2)\) of being in class 1, where \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\). That’s the two-class version of part 2’s softmax classifier, called logistic regression. The loss is the same cross-entropy, averaged over the points, plus a little L2 regularisation.

Now every pair \((w_1, w_2)\) is one complete classifier, and its loss is one number. Paint every pair by its loss, and we have a map: darker is lower.

Downhill, step by step

This is the loss of every classifier we could pick. The horizontal axis is \(w_1\), the vertical axis \(w_2\), and the shading is the loss: darker bands are lower.

The lowest point, ★, is at (0.75, 0.82) with loss 0.463. Our start, the ringed dot, is at (2.60, −3.50) with loss 0.790.

The low ground is a long, narrow valley: walls that rise fast across it, and a floor that falls only slowly along it. That shape makes optimisation hard, and it’s typical. Here it comes from the data: \(x_1\) is spread about eight times wider than \(x_2\), so changing \(w_1\) changes the scores much more than changing \(w_2\).

Click anywhere on the landscape to start from somewhere else; every later step reruns from there.

The simplest search: try random weights, and keep the best.

On this map it works fine. After 100 tries the best guess has loss 0.468, close to the lowest possible 0.463.

But it can’t scale. To land within a small distance of the best point, random guesses need to cover the space, and the number of guesses needed grows exponentially with the number of weights (the curse of dimensionality from part 1). With 12,292 weights, never mind millions, random search goes nowhere.

Better: stand where you are, and feel the slope. The gradient \( abla L = (\partial L / \partial w_1,\, \partial L / \partial w_2)\) is the direction in which the loss rises fastest. So minus the gradient points steepest downhill. The arrow shows it.

There are two ways to get it:

  • Numerically: nudge each weight by a tiny \(h\) and see how much the loss changes, \( rac{L(w + h) - L(w)}{h}\). Easy, but it costs one extra loss evaluation per weight: impossible with millions of weights.
  • Analytically: work out the formula with calculus. For this loss it’s \( abla L = rac{1}{N}\sum_i (p_i - y_i)\, x_i + \lambda w\). Exact and fast.

Here both give (0.2154, −0.0335): the two arrows lie on top of each other. In practice you always use the formula, and check it against the numerical version on a few weights. That’s a gradient check.

Gradient descent takes a small step against the gradient, recomputes it, and repeats:

\[w \leftarrow w - \eta\, abla L(w)\]

The step size \(\eta\) is the learning rate. Here \(\eta\) = 2.

Watch the path. It heads mostly across the valley first, because that’s where the slope is steepest, then turns and creeps along the floor, where the slope is gentle. After 60 steps the loss is down from 0.790 to 0.469; it took 49 steps to get within 0.01 of the lowest point.

Choose the learning rate below the figure. It’s the single most important setting in training a network.

  • 0.5: every step is safe but tiny. After 60 steps the loss is still 0.525.
  • 2: steady progress, as before.
  • 8: steps are big enough to overshoot the valley’s floor, and the path bounces from wall to wall. Sometimes the loss goes up.
  • 12: the first big step flings the weights far up the far wall (loss 3.54 after two steps). It finds its way back, but erratically.

Too small wastes time; too big wastes it in a different way, and on a less forgiving landscape it can make the loss grow without limit. The best value sits just below the point where the path starts to bounce.

Each gradient above used all 80 points. On ImageNet, the dataset most vision models are trained on, that would be 1.2 million images for every single step.

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) estimates the gradient from a small random minibatch instead, and takes a step with that. The estimate is noisy, but it’s cheap, so you can take far more steps for the same work.

With a batch of 8 points, the path swings widely around the full-gradient one, and the loss jumps up now and then, but it drifts the same way. With a batch of 32 it’s steadier; with a batch of 1, it staggers. The noise shrinks as the batch grows, roughly as one over the square root of its size. Real networks use batches of 32 to a few thousand images, and almost always train with some form of SGD.

Plain gradient descent forgets its past. In a narrow valley that’s a problem: it keeps stepping across the valley, and makes slow progress along it.

Momentum treats the weights like a ball rolling downhill. It keeps a running velocity \(v\), adds each new gradient to it, and steps along the velocity:

\[v \leftarrow eta v + abla L(w), \qquad w \leftarrow w - \eta\, v\]

With \( eta = 0.9\), the gradients along the valley point the same way every time and add up, so the ball picks up speed along the floor. The gradients across it flip sign from step to step, so they partly cancel. You can see both: the path swings from wall to wall, but it races up the valley while it does. It gets within 0.01 of the lowest loss after 44 steps, against 49 for plain descent.

Momentum isn’t magic: those swings show it can overshoot, and its loss curve is bumpier. Its strength shows most on long, gentle slopes, which deep networks have plenty of.

The valley is hard because one learning rate has to suit both weights. Steep \(w_1\) wants small steps; gentle \(w_2\) wants big ones.

Adam keeps two running averages for each weight: one of its gradients (momentum, as before), and one of its squared gradients. It divides the first by the square root of the second. A weight whose gradients are big gets smaller steps; one whose gradients are small gets bigger ones.

Here Adam with learning rate 0.1 gets within 0.01 of the lowest loss after 36 steps. It’s the default choice for most networks today, often in a variant called AdamW.

The whole thing in one line

Every method here repeats one loop:

  1. Take a minibatch of training examples.
  2. Compute the loss on it, and its gradient with respect to every weight.
  3. Update the weights using the gradient.

They differ only in step 3:

method update remembers
SGD \(w \leftarrow w - \eta\, g\) nothing
momentum \(v \leftarrow eta v + g,\; w \leftarrow w - \eta\, v\) a velocity per weight
Adam \(w \leftarrow w - \eta\, \hat m / (\sqrt{\hat v} + \epsilon)\) two averages per weight

Here \(g\) is the minibatch gradient. Adam’s \(\hat m\) and \(\hat v\) are given below.

What’s still missing

Step 2 needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. For our two weights, and for part 2’s linear classifier, a formula worked out by hand does it.

For a deep network, writing that formula by hand is hopeless. Part 4 shows how to get every gradient of any network mechanically, at about the cost of computing the loss once: backpropagation. Then we’ll use it to train our first neural network.

Going deeper

Why minus the gradient is steepest downhill

Take a tiny step \(\delta\) from \(w\). To first order, the loss changes by

\[L(w + \delta) - L(w) \approx abla L(w) \cdot \delta = \lVert abla L Vert\, \lVert \delta Vert \cos heta\]

where \( heta\) is the angle between the step and the gradient. For steps of a fixed length, this is most negative when \(\cos heta = -1\): pointing exactly against the gradient. That’s also why the gradient is at right angles to the contour lines: a step along a contour, \(\cos heta = 0\), doesn’t change the loss.

Numerical gradients and their error

The one-sided difference \( rac{L(w + h) - L(w)}{h}\) has an error proportional to \(h\). The centred difference

\[ rac{L(w + h) - L(w - h)}{2h}\]

has an error proportional to \(h^2\), because the second-order terms of the two Taylor expansions cancel. It costs two loss evaluations instead of one, and it’s what CS231n recommends for gradient checks. Make \(h\) too small, though, and floating-point rounding takes over; around \(10^{-5}\) is typical.

Compare the two by relative error, \( rac{\lvert a - n vert}{\max(\lvert a vert, \lvert n vert)}\): below about \(10^{-7}\) is a pass; above \(10^{-2}\) means the analytic gradient is probably wrong.

Why the valley is narrow, and how to widen it

Near the bottom, the loss looks like a bowl, \(L(w) \approx L(w^*) + rac{1}{2}(w - w^*)^ op H (w - w^*)\), where \(H\) is the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives. The curvature along each direction is an eigenvalue of \(H\).

Here the steep direction curves about 28 times more than the gentle one. Gradient descent is stable only if \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\), set by the steepest direction, but then it crawls along the gentlest one, at a rate set by the ratio \(\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\), the condition number.

For a linear model the curvature comes straight from the spread of the inputs. Standardising each input (subtract its mean, divide by its standard deviation) makes the bowl rounder before training even starts. That’s why image pixels are normalised before they go into a network, and it’s the same idea as batch normalisation, later in the course.

Learning-rate schedules

A rate that’s right at the start is usually too big near the end, where the minibatch noise makes the weights jitter around the minimum. So the learning rate is lowered during training:

  • step decay: divide by 10 at a few fixed epochs (the classic recipe for ResNets);
  • cosine decay: follow half a cosine from the initial rate down to 0;
  • warm-up: start from a very small rate and raise it over the first few hundred steps, which keeps early, wild gradients from wrecking the initial weights. Transformers almost always use it.

Adam in full

For each weight, with gradient \(g_t\) at step \(t\):

\[m_t = eta_1 m_{t-1} + (1 - eta_1)\, g_t \qquad v_t = eta_2 v_{t-1} + (1 - eta_2)\, g_t^2\] \[\hat m_t = rac{m_t}{1 - eta_1^t} \qquad \hat v_t = rac{v_t}{1 - eta_2^t} \qquad w_t = w_{t-1} - \eta\, rac{\hat m_t}{\sqrt{\hat v_t} + \epsilon}\]

with the usual \( eta_1 = 0.9\), \( eta_2 = 0.999\) and \(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\). The hats are a bias correction: \(m\) and \(v\) start at 0, so in the first steps they underestimate the true averages, and dividing by \(1 - eta^t\) undoes that.

Without \(m\), the method is RMSProp (Hinton’s lecture notes, 2012). Without \(v\), it’s momentum. AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) applies weight decay directly to the weights instead of adding it to the gradient, which works better with Adam’s per-weight scaling.

Why not use the curvature directly?

Newton’s method steps by \(w \leftarrow w - H^{-1} abla L\). On a bowl it jumps to the bottom in a single step, whatever the condition number. But \(H\) has one entry per pair of weights: for a network with 10 million weights, that’s \(10^{14}\) numbers, and inverting it is out of the question. Approximations such as L-BFGS work well on small problems with full batches; for deep networks, cheap first-order methods with minibatches have won.

Further reading

  • CS231n notes, Optimization: Stochastic Gradient Descent and the training section of Neural Networks Part 3: gradient checks, momentum, Adam and schedules.
  • D. Kingma and J. Ba, Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization (2015).
  • I. Loshchilov and F. Hutter, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (2019): AdamW.
  • G. Goh, Why Momentum Really Works (Distill, 2017): an interactive look at momentum on narrow valleys.

entry.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 4: backpropagation and neural networks

link.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 4: backpropagation and neural networks

entry.content:
Series · Deep learning for computer vision 1Image classification and nearest neighbours 2Linear classifiers and loss functions 3Optimisation 4Backpropagation and neural networks 5Convolutional networks 6Visualising and understanding 7CNN architectures · soon 8Detection and segmentation · soon 9Vision transformers · soon

Part 3 trained weights by repeating one loop: compute the loss, compute its gradient, step downhill. For two weights, and for a linear classifier, we could write the gradient’s formula by hand.

A neural network has millions of weights, stacked in layers. Writing its gradient by hand is hopeless. Backpropagation computes all of it mechanically, from local rules that each fit on one line, at roughly the cost of computing the loss once. This part follows CS231n’s notes on backpropagation and neural networks, and ends by training a network in your browser.

Gradients, one gate at a time

Any formula can be broken into tiny operations. Take \(f(x, y, z) = (x + y)\,z\). Name the middle result \(q = x + y\), so \(f = q\,z\).

Each circle is a gate: it takes its inputs and computes one simple thing. The forward pass runs left to right and writes each result, in green, on the edge leaving the gate.

With \(x = -2\), \(y = 5\) and \(z = -4\): \(q = 3\) and \(f = -12\).

We want \(\partial f/\partial x\), \(\partial f/\partial y\) and \(\partial f/\partial z\): how much \(f\) changes when each input is nudged.

The backward pass runs right to left and writes each gradient in red, under the edge:

  1. At the output, \(\partial f/\partial f = 1\).
  2. The multiply gate \(f = qz\) knows its own derivatives: \(\partial f/\partial q = z = -4\) and \(\partial f/\partial z = q = 3\).
  3. The add gate \(q = x + y\) has derivative 1 for both inputs. So \(\partial f/\partial x = \partial f/\partial y = 1 \times (-4) = -4\).

Read it as: raising \(x\) by a little \(h\) lowers \(f\) by about \(4h\).

Step 3 was the chain rule: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial q}\cdot\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}\).

What makes backpropagation work is that no gate needs to see the whole graph. During the backward pass each gate receives one number from above, the gradient of the final output with respect to its own output (the upstream gradient). It multiplies that by its own local gradient, which it can work out from its inputs alone, and passes the result down to each input:

\[\text{downstream} = \text{local} \times \text{upstream}\]

Where an input feeds several gates, the gradients arriving back from them add up.

A bigger example: a single neuron with a sigmoid.

\[f(w, x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w_0 x_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2)}}\]

Cut into the smallest pieces: two multiplies, two adds, then \(\times -1\), \(\exp\), \(+1\) and \(1/x\). With \(w = (2, -3, -3)\) and \(x = (-1, -2)\), the forward pass gives a weighted sum of 1, and \(f = 0.731\).

Keep scrolling to watch the backward pass. Each gate uses only its local rule: \(1/x\) has derivative \(-1/x^2\), \(\exp\) has derivative \(e^x\), and so on. At the end, \(\partial f/\partial w = (-0.197, -0.393, 0.197)\) and \(\partial f/\partial x = (0.393, -0.590)\).

Notice the gradient arriving at the weighted sum, 0.197. That’s \(\sigma(1)\,(1 - \sigma(1)) = 0.731 \times 0.269\): the last four gates together are the sigmoid, and its derivative is \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\). In practice the whole sigmoid is one gate with that rule. How finely to cut the graph is up to you, as long as each gate knows its local gradient.

The gradient flowing backwards follows simple patterns. Take \(f = 2\,(xy + \max(z, w))\) with \(x = 3\), \(y = -4\), \(z = 2\) and \(w = -1\). The gradient arriving at the add gate is 2.

  • The add gate distributes: it passes the gradient unchanged to every input. Both branches get 2.
  • The max gate routes: the whole gradient goes to whichever input was larger, \(z\); the other, \(w\), gets 0. Nudging \(w\) a little wouldn’t change the max at all.
  • The multiply gate swaps: each input gets the other input’s value times the gradient. \(x\) gets \(-4 \times 2 = -8\), \(y\) gets \(3 \times 2 = 6\).

The swap has a practical side. If one input is very large, the other input’s gradient is very large too. That’s one reason inputs are normalised before training.

Back to part 2’s spiral: three arms of 60 points. A linear classifier draws straight borders and gets 52% right.

A two-layer neural network puts one more step in the middle:

\[s = W_2 \max(0,\; W_1 x + b_1) + b_2\]

\(W_1\) maps the 2 inputs to 40 hidden units. The \(\max(0, \cdot)\), called ReLU, sets every negative hidden value to 0. Then \(W_2\) maps the hidden units to 3 class scores, exactly like part 2’s classifier.

Without the ReLU the two matrices would multiply into one, \(W_2 W_1\), and the network would still be linear. The non-linearity is what buys the extra power. Here it gets 98.9% of the points right.

Nothing about training is new. Softmax loss from part 2, plus L2 regularisation. Gradients from backpropagation: the network is just a graph of multiplies, adds and maxes. Updates from part 3’s Adam, with learning rate 0.02.

Keep scrolling to train it. The weights start random, at 26% (about chance for three classes). By step 50 the network gets 80% right; by step 100, 96%. The loss falls from 1.45 to 0.26 over 600 steps.

The whole run takes a fraction of a second in your browser.

More hidden units, more complicated borders. Pick a width below the chart.

With 2 hidden units the network gets 49% right, no better than the linear classifier. With 5 it jumps to 96%; 10 gives 98% and 40 gives 99%.

More units means more capacity, which also means more room to overfit. CS231n’s advice is not to shrink the network to avoid overfitting, but to use a big enough network and control it with regularisation (part 2’s \(\lambda\)), because big networks are easier to train well.

Each hidden unit is a linear classifier of its own. Unit \(k\) computes \(\max(0, w_k \cdot x + b_k)\): zero on one side of the line \(w_k \cdot x + b_k = 0\), and growing with distance on the other.

The lines here are the 5 units of the 5-unit network. Every border in the tinted map is built from pieces of them: the output layer adds up these bent ramps, with its own weights, to make each class’s score.

That’s the network’s whole trick. Layers of simple bent pieces, combined, can approximate almost any shape.

The whole thing in one line

Backpropagation is the chain rule, applied in the right order:

  1. Forward: compute every gate’s output, left to right, and keep them.
  2. Backward: start from \(\partial L/\partial L = 1\) and, right to left, give each gate’s inputs \(\text{local gradient} \times \text{upstream gradient}\), adding where paths meet.

Each step costs about as much as the forward pass, whatever the number of weights. That’s why the loop from part 3 still works with millions of them.

gate forward backward (upstream \(g\))
add \(a + b\) \(g\) to both
multiply \(a \cdot b\) \(b\,g\) to \(a\), \(a\,g\) to \(b\)
max \(\max(a, b)\) \(g\) to the larger, 0 to the other
ReLU \(\max(0, a)\) \(g\) if \(a > 0\), else 0

What’s still missing

The network here takes 2 numbers. An image is thousands of pixels, and a fully connected hidden layer gives every unit one weight per pixel. For a 200 × 200 colour image that’s 120,000 weights per unit, and none of them knows that neighbouring pixels belong together, or that an edge on the left is the same kind of thing as an edge on the right.

Part 5 builds both into the layer with convolutional layers: small filters, each looking at a few neighbouring pixels, and each shared across the whole image.

Going deeper

Gradients of matrices

In a real network the gates take whole matrices. For \(Y = XW\), with \(X\) of shape \(N \times D\) and \(W\) of shape \(D \times M\), and upstream gradient \(\partial L/\partial Y\) of shape \(N \times M\):

\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = X^\top \frac{\partial L}{\partial Y} \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial X} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial Y}\, W^\top\]

You rarely need to derive these. Check the shapes: the gradient has the same shape as the thing it’s for, and there’s usually only one way to multiply the pieces to get it. That’s the trick the CS231n notes recommend.

Activation functions

  • Sigmoid squashes to \((0, 1)\), but its gradient \(\sigma(1 - \sigma)\) is at most 0.25 and near 0 for large inputs, so gradients vanish through many layers. Its outputs are also always positive.
  • tanh is a zero-centred sigmoid, with the same vanishing problem.
  • ReLU, \(\max(0, x)\), has gradient 1 wherever it’s on. It’s cheap and trains fast (Krizhevsky et al., 2012 reported about six times faster than tanh). Its weakness: a unit that is off for every input gets no gradient and never recovers, a dead ReLU.
  • Leaky ReLU and GELU keep a little gradient for negative inputs. GELU is the default in transformers.

Initialisation

If all weights start equal, every hidden unit computes the same thing and gets the same gradient, forever. So weights start random. Their scale matters too: too small and the signal shrinks layer by layer, too large and it explodes. He initialisation (He et al., 2015) draws each weight with variance \(2/n_\text{in}\), which keeps the signal’s size steady through ReLU layers. The network here uses it.

Automatic differentiation

Modern libraries such as PyTorch and JAX record the graph as your code runs, and backpropagate through it on request (loss.backward()). That’s reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Each operation is implemented once with its forward and backward rule, exactly the gates above, and the library does the bookkeeping.

entry.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 5: convolutional networks

link.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 5: convolutional networks

entry.content:
Series · Deep learning for computer vision 1Image classification and nearest neighbours 2Linear classifiers and loss functions 3Optimisation 4Backpropagation and neural networks 5Convolutional networks 6Visualising and understanding 7CNN architectures · soon 8Detection and segmentation · soon 9Vision transformers · soon

Part 4 trained a neural network on 2 numbers. Images have far more. A fully connected layer gives each hidden unit one weight per input: 3,072 for our 32 × 32 colour photos, and 120,000 for a 200 × 200 one, per unit.

Worse, those weights don’t know anything about images. They don’t know that neighbouring pixels belong together, or that an edge on the left is the same kind of thing as an edge on the right. Part 2’s linear classifier showed what that costs: it had to learn one whole-photo template per class, a blur of every plane it had seen.

Convolutional networks build both facts into the layer itself. This part follows CS231n’s notes on convolutional networks, using the same CIFAR-10 photos of planes, cars, frogs and ships as parts 1 and 2.

A filter that slides

A filter is a tiny grid of weights, here 3 × 3. This one has a column of −1 on the left, 0 in the middle and +1 on the right. Laid over a 3 × 3 patch of the image, it multiplies each pixel by its weight and adds them up.

We use the photo’s brightness, minus its average brightness, so each pixel is a number around 0. Where the patch is the same all over, the −1s and +1s cancel and the sum is about 0. Where it gets brighter from left to right, the +1s win and the sum is positive; where it gets darker, negative. So this filter finds vertical edges.

The ringed cell on the right is where it responds most strongly in this photo: 1.74, beside the police car’s front wheel, where the dark tyre gives way to the light body. The building’s columns light up too. Use the arrows above to try other test photos, and the menu below to try other filters.

Convolution is that one sum, at every position. Keep scrolling to slide the window across the photo, one row at a time. Each position gives one number of the output.

The output is a feature map: an image of where the filter found what it looks for. Red where it matched, blue where the opposite pattern was.

The key idea is that every position uses the same 9 weights. A fully connected layer would need 1,024 weights for each output; this needs 9 for all of them. That’s weight sharing. And each output looks only at its own 3 × 3 neighbourhood, its receptive field.

The dashed ring around the photo is zero padding: one border of zeros, so the window can be centred on the edge pixels too, and the output stays 32 × 32. Because we subtracted the average brightness first, a zero is an average grey. With raw brightness from 0 to 1, the padding would be black, and every bright photo would get a strong false edge all the way round.

A layer has many filters, each producing its own map. Here are four hand-made edge filters: vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals. Each map has been passed through ReLU, as in part 4, so only the positive responses remain.

Stacked together, the maps are the layer’s output: a block 32 × 32 × 4, which the next layer reads as an image with 4 channels. A real network’s first layer has dozens of filters, each spanning all 3 colour channels: a 3 × 3 filter on a colour photo has 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 weights.

Each map shows a different part of the picture. The vertical map picks out the building’s columns and the edges of the wheels; the horizontal map, the outline of the roof and the bottom of the body; the two diagonal maps, the two slopes of the roof.

None of this classifies anything yet. A network learns its own filters, and learns what to make of their maps, as we’ll see below.

Two settings change the output’s size. Padding \(P\) adds a border of zeros. Stride \(S\) is how far the window moves each time. For an input \(W\) pixels wide and a filter \(F\) wide, the output is

\[\frac{W - F + 2P}{S} + 1\]

pixels wide. Try the menus below:

  • padding 1, stride 1: \((32 - 3 + 2)/1 + 1 = 32\), the same size as the input;
  • padding 0, stride 1: \((32 - 3)/1 + 1 = 30\), so the map shrinks by 2 every layer;
  • padding 1, stride 2: \((32 - 3 + 2)/2 + 1 = 16.5\), which doesn’t divide evenly. Libraries round down to 16, quietly ignoring the last row and column of the padding.

Stride 2 halves the size: a cheap way to shrink the maps, which some networks use instead of pooling.

Max pooling shrinks a map by keeping only the largest value in each 2 × 2 block. Keep scrolling to watch it, one row of blocks at a time.

The 32 × 32 map becomes 16 × 16: a quarter of the numbers, with the strong responses kept. Pooling has no weights at all.

Shrinking matters because each later layer’s 3 × 3 filter then covers a bigger part of the original photo. Stack enough conv and pool layers and the last ones see the whole picture.

Move the photo right with the slider, and look at the feature map: it moves right by the same amount. The ringed response keeps its exact value, just a few columns over. Because the filter is the same everywhere, a shifted input gives a shifted output. That’s translation equivariance.

Except at the edges. The black strip the move leaves behind is itself a strong edge, and the map lights up along it.

That matters more than you might hope. Move all 100 test photos 4 pixels right, and the network below drops from 65% to 52%; part 2’s linear classifier drops from 67% to 58%. A convnet reuses what it learned at every position, but nothing makes the whole network ignore a black strip it never saw in training. Real networks learn that from data, as “Going deeper” explains.

We don’t hand-make filters in practice: they’re learned. The network here is small, but it’s a real convnet:

  1. 8 filters of 3 × 3 × 3 on the colour photo, with padding 1, then ReLU;
  2. a 2 × 2 max pool, giving 16 × 16 × 8;
  3. 16 filters of 3 × 3 × 8, then ReLU;
  4. the largest value of each of those 16 maps (a global max pool), giving 16 numbers;
  5. a linear classifier from those 16 numbers to 4 class scores.

It’s trained exactly like part 4’s network: softmax loss, backpropagation, Adam. During the backward pass, each max routes its gradient to the one position that won (part 4’s max gate), and from there into the filter weights below it.

Like part 2’s classifier, it was trained before you opened the page: 60 passes over the 320 training photos, each photo flipped left to right half the time, which is a free way to get more data (a car facing left is still a car). Its settings were picked on the validation photos, where it gets 74%.

The top row shows its first layer’s filters as tiny colour pictures, with their maps on the current photo. Some respond to edges, some to colours. On the test photos it gets 65%: 23 of 25 cars and 20 frogs, but only 8 planes.

Compare it to part 2’s linear classifier, top. That model needs a full 32 × 32 colour template per class: 12,292 parameters, and 67% of the test photos right.

The convnet, bottom, has 1,460 parameters, an eighth as many: 224 in the first layer, 1,168 in the second, and 68 in the linear layer. It gets 65%.

On 100 test photos those two numbers are too close to separate: one photo is one percentage point. On all 4,000 CIFAR-10 test photos of these four classes, the same two models get 59.7% (linear) and 67.5% (convnet). And with more training data the gap grows: trained on 1,000 photos per class instead of 80, the same convnet design reaches 76.9% on those 4,000 photos, and a linear classifier 64.8%.

An eighth of the parameters, about the same accuracy here, and better with more data, because the layer’s design matches what photos are like: local patterns that can appear anywhere. That built-in assumption is called an inductive bias.

The whole thing in one line

A convolutional layer takes a block of \(H \times W \times C\) numbers and applies \(K\) filters, each \(F \times F \times C\):

\[\text{out}[i, j, k] = b_k + \sum_{a, b, c} w_k[a, b, c] \cdot \text{in}[iS + a - P,\; jS + b - P,\; c]\]

That gives \(K\) feature maps, each \(\frac{W - F + 2P}{S} + 1\) wide, with \(K(F^2 C + 1)\) parameters in total, however big the image is. A convnet stacks conv layers with ReLU, shrinks the maps now and then with pooling or stride 2, and ends with a fully connected layer (or a global pool and one) that gives the scores.

layer weights output size from \(W \times W \times C\)
conv, \(K\) filters \(K(F^2C + 1)\) \(\frac{W - F + 2P}{S} + 1\), \(K\) channels
ReLU none the same
max pool, 2 × 2 none \(W/2\), \(C\) channels
fully connected one per input, per output a vector

What’s still missing

Our network has two conv layers and 24 filters, for four classes of tiny photos. Real photos need far more: AlexNet in 2012 had 5 conv layers and 60 million parameters, and newer networks go hundreds of layers deep.

Stacking many layers raises its own problems: gradients that vanish on the way back, and networks that train worse as they get deeper. Part 7 walks through the architectures that solved them, from AlexNet and VGG to ResNet’s skip connections.

First, part 6 trains a somewhat bigger network on more photos and looks inside it: which parts of a photo it uses, and how easily it’s fooled.

Going deeper

What the filters learn

On large photos and datasets, the first layer’s filters learn edges at various angles, and blobs of colour, much like the hand-made ones here. (Ours, trained on 320 photos, are rougher.) Zeiler and Fergus (2014) visualised deeper layers: the second responds to corners and textures, later ones to parts such as eyes and wheels, and the last ones to whole objects. Each layer combines the patterns of the layer below over a larger receptive field.

Receptive fields grow

One 3 × 3 conv sees 3 × 3 pixels. Two stacked see 5 × 5, three see 7 × 7. Three 3 × 3 layers cover the same area as one 7 × 7 layer, with fewer weights (\(3 \times 9 C^2 = 27C^2\) against \(49C^2\)) and two extra ReLUs in between. That’s the argument behind VGG’s all-3 × 3 design in part 7.

Equivariance, invariance, and their limits

A convolution is equivariant to shifts: shift the input, and the output shifts the same way. Pooling, especially global pooling, turns that into invariance: shift the input, and the output doesn’t change. Neither holds exactly in practice. Padding treats the edges differently, and a stride or pool of 2 means a one-pixel shift can change which values get kept. Zhang (2019) showed that real convnets are surprisingly sensitive to small shifts for this reason, and fixed much of it by blurring before each down-sampling.

Convolutions are not equivariant to rotation or scale. Networks learn those from data, usually helped by data augmentation: training on randomly flipped, cropped and rescaled copies of the images.

Convolution or cross-correlation?

Strictly, the operation here is a cross-correlation. A mathematical convolution flips the filter first. Deep-learning libraries skip the flip and still call it convolution; since the filters are learned, it makes no difference.

  • CS231n notes, Convolutional Neural Networks: the layer sizes, the output-size formula and the parameter counts.
  • A. Krizhevsky, Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images (2009): the CIFAR-10 dataset our photos come from.
  • Y. LeCun, L. Bottou, Y. Bengio and P. Haffner, Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition (1998): LeNet-5, the convnet that read cheques.
  • M. Zeiler and R. Fergus, Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks (2014).
  • V. Dumoulin and F. Visin, A guide to convolution arithmetic for deep learning (2016): pictures of every combination of padding and stride.

entry.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 6: visualising and understanding

link.title: deep learning for computer vision, part 6: visualising and understanding

entry.content:
Series · Deep learning for computer vision 1Image classification and nearest neighbours 2Linear classifiers and loss functions 3Optimisation 4Backpropagation and neural networks 5Convolutional networks 6Visualising and understanding 7CNN architectures · soon 8Detection and segmentation · soon 9Vision transformers · soon

Part 5 trained a convnet and measured how often it was right. That doesn’t tell us why it was right: which parts of the photo it used, or whether it learned what we hoped it would.

This part opens a trained network up, following CS231n’s lecture on visualising and understanding convnets. The pictures it produces are often called attention maps, or more precisely attribution or saliency maps: for each part of the photo, how much it counted towards the answer. (A network that attends, with a layer that decides where to look, comes in part 9 with vision transformers.)

Part 5’s network is too weak to be worth inspecting: it gets 65% of the test photos right, and covering a patch at the border of a photo costs it about as much as covering one in the middle (on average, 0.029 off the probability of the right class, against 0.027). So we train a bigger one on more photos.

Inside a trained network

The network here is part 5’s, made deeper and trained on more photos:

  1. 16 filters of 3 × 3 × 3, ReLU, a 2 × 2 max pool: 16 × 16 × 16;
  2. 32 filters of 3 × 3 × 16, ReLU, a 2 × 2 max pool: 8 × 8 × 32;
  3. 64 filters of 3 × 3 × 32, ReLU: 8 × 8 × 64;
  4. the average of each of those 64 maps (a global average pool), and a linear layer to the 4 scores.

That’s 23,844 weights. It was trained offline on 19,920 CIFAR-10 photos of the same four classes, every training photo except the 80 validation ones, for 40 passes. Each photo was flipped half the time and moved by up to 4 pixels.

It gets 92 of our 100 test photos right, and 89.8% of all 4,000 CIFAR-10 test photos of these classes. The pictures show one map from each layer: the first layer’s maps still look like the photo, and the last layer’s are coarse 8 × 8 grids.

The scores come from the last layer’s 64 maps. Each map is averaged to a single number, and each class’s score is a weighted sum of those 64 averages, plus a bias:

\[s_j = b_j + \sum_k w_{jk} \cdot \operatorname{avg}(A_k)\]

The pictures are the 12 maps with the biggest effect on the class picked in the menu, each with its contribution \(w_{jk} \cdot \operatorname{avg}(A_k)\) under it. Positive ones push the score up, negative ones down.

A single map is hard to read on its own. Together, though, they hold all the evidence the network has.

Swap the order: weight the maps first, average after. Since averaging is linear, it gives the same score:

\[s_j = b_j + \operatorname{avg}\Big(\sum_k w_{jk} A_k\Big)\]

The weighted sum inside the brackets is an 8 × 8 map, the class activation map or CAM (Zhou et al., 2016). Each cell says how much that part of the photo adds to the class’s score: red for evidence for, blue for evidence against. Its average, plus the bias, is the score exactly.

Here it is for all four classes, stretched over the photo. Look at where the “plane” evidence sits. For this plane, it’s mostly on the white sky around the plane, not on the plane itself.

That’s not a one-off. We measured, for each 4 × 4 block of a photo, how plain it is (how little its pixels vary). On 82% of the 1,000 plane test photos, the plane CAM is higher on the plainer blocks. The car CAM is the opposite: higher on the busier blocks, on 93% of the car photos.

A CAM needs a network built this way. Occlusion works on any. Cover part of the photo with a grey patch, run the network again, and see how far the probability of the right class falls (Zeiler and Fergus, 2014). Keep scrolling to slide an 8 × 8 patch across the photo, 4 pixels at a time: 49 positions, 49 more runs of the network.

Red cells mark where covering the photo hurt. For this plane, no single patch matters much: the worst drops it from 100% to 89%. The evidence is spread out.

Other photos are more fragile. In test photo 4, a ship, covering a patch of the hull turns the answer into “car”, at 96%.

The patch’s colour matters too. It’s the training photos’ average colour, which is zero to the network, but zero isn’t “nothing” to it: a photo that’s all that grey comes out 62% ship and 28% plane.

A third way: ask how the score would change if each pixel changed a little. That’s the gradient of the score with respect to the pixels, found with one backward pass (Simonyan et al., 2014), exactly as in part 4, but stopping at the photo instead of the weights. The middle picture shows its size at each pixel.

It’s sharp, but noisy, and it says less about the class than you’d hope. Pick another class in the menu: the gradient map hardly changes. Across our 100 test photos, the gradient maps for the photo’s own class and for another class have a rank correlation of 0.43. The two CAMs have −0.23: evidence for one class tends to be evidence against another.

A gradient is a local answer: what tiny changes to each pixel would do. It doesn’t say what the network relied on.

Do these maps show the network, or just the photo? Adebayo et al. (2018) proposed a simple test: compute the same map for a network with random weights. If it looks the same, the map shows what’s in the photo, such as its edges, not what was learned.

The bottom row is the same network with random weights. For this plane, the random CAM still has a rough plane-against-sky shape (rank correlation 0.48 with the trained one): random filters respond to bright, flat regions too.

Averaged over all 100 test photos, though, the trained and random maps have little in common: a rank correlation of 0.16 for the gradient maps, and 0.05 for the CAMs. Both depend on what the network learned, so both pass. Several popular methods don’t; see “Going deeper”.

The confusion matrix counts, for each true class, what the network said. On our 100 test photos, it makes 8 mistakes; 5 of them are planes.

Planes are its weakest class on all 4,000 test photos too: 84.5% right, against 95.9% for frogs. The biggest confusions are between the two classes with large, plain backgrounds: 84 planes called ships, and 82 ships called planes. A plane over the sea and a ship under a pale sky share most of their pixels.

The heat on each mistake is the CAM for the wrong answer: what it took as evidence for that class.

The maps suggest things. Changing the photos tests them. Each edit in the menu is applied here to the current photo, and was measured on all 4,000 test photos:

edit right, of 4,000
unchanged 89.8%
centre hidden (16 × 16 of 32 × 32) 70.6%
only the centre kept 44.3%
greyscale 84.3%
red and blue swapped 62.8%
moved 8 px right 87.1%

With the centre hidden, where the object usually is, it still gets 70.6% right, and 78.7% of ships: much of what it uses is around the object. Keep only the centre, with grey all round, and it calls 77% of all the photos “plane”. To this network, a plain surround means a plane.

Colour matters most for frogs: swap red and blue, and only 33.7% of frogs are still frogs. Moving the photo costs little, because it was trained on moved photos; part 5’s network fell to 46% at 8 pixels.

The gradient also says how to make the network wrong. Move every pixel’s colours a tiny step, \(\epsilon\), in the direction that increases the loss:

\[x' = x + \epsilon \cdot \operatorname{sign}\big(\nabla_x L\big)\]

This is the fast gradient sign method (Goodfellow et al., 2015). At \(\epsilon = 2/255\), the nudged photo looks the same as the original, but on all 4,000 test photos accuracy falls from 89.8% to 66.1%. At 8/255 it’s 20.1%: worse than guessing.

This plane holds: it stays a plane even at 8/255. Of the 92 test photos the network gets right, 25 change their answer at 2/255 or less, and 75 at 8/255 or less. Try test photo 4, the ship: at 2/255, it’s a car.

These are adversarial examples (Szegedy et al., 2014). The change is chosen with the gradient, so it’s tiny on every pixel, but every pixel pushes the same way.

What we learned about this network

The network is right 89.8% of the time, but not always for reasons we’d choose:

  • It reads the background. The CAMs put much of the evidence for “plane” on the sky, and the edits agree: hide the object and it’s still right 70.6% of the time; surround any object with plain grey and it’s usually a plane.
  • Its biggest confusion is plane against ship, the two classes with large plain backgrounds.
  • Colour is a big clue for frogs, and much less for the others.
  • It tolerates moves and flips it was trained on, and not small, chosen changes it wasn’t.

None of this is a bug in the code. The network learned what the training photos rewarded. In our training photos, 43% of the border of a plane photo is almost flat colour, against 33% for ships, 18% for cars and 12% for frogs. A network that has learned a shortcut like this can score well on a test set that shares it, and fail in the world.

Every map here is a hypothesis about the network, not proof. The edits and the sanity check are what turn a picture into evidence.

Going deeper

Grad-CAM, for any convnet

The CAM needs a global average pool straight before the last linear layer. Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., 2017) removes the restriction: it weights each map by the average gradient of the score with respect to that map. For a network like ours, that average is \(w_{jk}/64\), so Grad-CAM gives the CAM back, scaled down, with its negative parts set to zero. It’s one of the methods that passes the sanity check.

Smoother gradients

Raw gradients are noisy because ReLU networks are piecewise linear: the gradient jumps as each unit switches on or off. SmoothGrad (Smilkov et al., 2017) averages the gradient over many noisy copies of the photo. Integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017) adds up gradients along a path from a plain baseline image to the photo, so the contributions add up to the change in score. Both need choices: how much noise, which baseline. Grey, as we saw, isn’t neutral.

Some methods, such as guided backpropagation, make sharper pictures, but Adebayo et al. found they barely change when the weights are randomised: they show the photo’s edges, not the model.

What a unit wants to see

Instead of asking about one photo, we can ask about one unit: start from noise and follow the gradient to make a picture that excites it as much as possible (Simonyan et al., 2014; Olah et al., 2017). Without strong regularisation, the result is itself an adversarial pattern. With it, large networks give recognisable textures, parts and objects, layer by layer. Another way is to show the training photos that excite a unit most.

Shortcuts

The plane-and-sky shortcut has well-known relatives. One classifier told wolves from huskies by the snow in the background (Ribeiro et al., 2016). ImageNet networks rely more on texture than on shape (Geirhos et al., 2019). Geirhos et al. (2020) collect many examples under the name shortcut learning.

Defending against adversarial examples

The most reliable defence is adversarial training: generate adversarial examples while training, and train on them too (Madry et al., 2018). It costs accuracy on clean photos and many times the compute. Goodfellow et al. argued that adversarial examples come from networks being too linear: thousands of tiny changes, each aligned with a weight, add up to a large change in the score. That’s why the sign of the gradient, rather than the gradient itself, works so well.

Further reading

  • CS231n notes, Visualizing what ConvNets learn.
  • B. Zhou, A. Khosla, A. Lapedriza, A. Oliva and A. Torralba, Learning Deep Features for Discriminative Localization (2016): the class activation map.
  • M. Zeiler and R. Fergus, Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks (2014): occlusion, and pictures of what each layer responds to.
  • K. Simonyan, A. Vedaldi and A. Zisserman, Deep Inside Convolutional Networks (2014): gradient saliency maps.
  • J. Adebayo et al., Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps (2018).
  • I. Goodfellow, J. Shlens and C. Szegedy, Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples (2015).
  • A. Krizhevsky, Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images (2009): the CIFAR-10 dataset our photos come from.
